p-values-s1.title: Pastries with coffee
p-values-s1.text: A coffee chain's head office says that 40% of its customers order a pastry. A store manager suspects the proportion at her store is lower. She selects a random sample of 300 orders from the store's many orders this month, and 105 of them include a pastry. She tests $H_0: p = 0.40$ against $H_a: p < 0.40$, where $p$ is the true proportion of all the store's orders this month that include a pastry. The conditions are met.

p-values-s2.title: Simulating free throws
p-values-s2.text: A coach says a player makes 75% of her free throws. In one week of practice she makes 31 of 50 ($\hat{p} = 0.62$), and a teammate wonders whether her true rate is lower. To test $H_0: p = 0.75$ against $H_a: p < 0.75$, a computer simulates 100 sets of 50 shots by a player who makes each shot with probability 0.75. Each dot is the proportion made in one simulated set.

plot.label: Dotplot of 100 simulated proportions of free throws made out of 50, assuming a 75% shooter; 3 dots are at or below 0.62
plot.xLabel: simulated proportion of 50 free throws made

items.q: Calculate the standardized test statistic. Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses $\hat{p} = 0.35$ inside the square root. A test's standard deviation uses $p_0 = 0.40$: $\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/300}$.
The sign is backward. Compute statistic minus null value, $0.35 - 0.40$, which is negative.
That divides by $\frac{0.40(0.60)}{300}$ with no square root. The denominator is a standard deviation: $\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/300} = 0.0283$.

why.correct: $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}} = \frac{0.35 - 0.40}{\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/300}} = \frac{-0.05}{0.0283} = -1.77$. The standard deviation uses $p_0$, because the test assumes $H_0$ is true.

items.q: Type the expression for the test statistic with the values substituted, as you would show it on the exam.

mistakes.why: Use $p_0 = 0.40$ in the standard deviation of a test, not $\hat{p} = 0.35$.
The standard deviation needs a square root around $\frac{0.40(0.60)}{300}$.
Subtract in the order statistic minus null value: $0.35 - 0.40$.

why.correct: (statistic − null value) / (standard deviation of the statistic): $\frac{0.35 - 0.40}{\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/300}}$.

items.q: Find the p-value of the test. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That doubles the tail area, as for a two-sided test. Here $H_a: p < 0.40$ is one-sided, so use one tail.
That is the area to the right of $z = -1.77$. The alternative says "less than", so shade the left tail.

why.correct: $H_a$ is $p < 0.40$, so the p-value is the area to the left of $z = -1.77$: $P(Z \le -1.77) = 0.0385$. Technology (a 1-proportion z test) gives 0.0385. Table A with $z = -1.77$ gives 0.0384.

items.q: Build the interpretation of the p-value, 0.0385, in context.

options: Assuming the true proportion of all the store's orders that include a pastry is 0.40,
Assuming the true proportion of all the store's orders that include a pastry is 0.35,
Assuming the manager is right that the proportion is lower,

why.1: The p-value is computed assuming the null value, 0.40, not the sample result.
why.2: The p-value assumes $H_0$ is true, not $H_a$.

options: there is a 0.0385 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.35 or less
there is a 0.0385 probability that the null hypothesis is true
there is a 0.0385 probability of getting a sample proportion of exactly 0.35

why.1: A p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true; it is computed by assuming $H_0$ is true.
why.2: It is the probability of a result as extreme or more, "0.35 or less", not exactly 0.35.

options: by chance in a random sample of 300 orders.
in the store's orders next month.
in the 105 orders that included a pastry.

why.1: The p-value is about random samples of the same size, 300 orders, not next month's orders.
why.2: The 105 orders are the result, not the sample the probability describes.

conclude.model: Assuming the true proportion of all the store's orders that include a pastry is 0.40, there is a 0.0385 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.35 or less by chance in a random sample of 300 orders.

why.correct: A p-value is a probability computed assuming $H_0$ is true: the chance of a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction of $H_a$.

items.q: What does the small p-value, 0.0385, suggest?
options: This result is unusual if $p = 0.40$, which is evidence that $p < 0.40$
There is a 3.85% chance that the head office's figure of 40% is correct
About 3.85% of the store's orders include a pastry
The manager has proven that fewer than 40% of orders include a pastry

why.correct: If the true proportion were 0.40, a sample proportion as low as 0.35 would happen only about 4% of the time. That makes 0.40 hard to believe, which is evidence for $H_a: p < 0.40$.
options: Right: a small p-value counts against $H_0$ and for $H_a$.
The p-value assumes the figure is correct; it is not the probability that it is.
The p-value is a probability about samples, not a proportion of orders.
A small p-value is evidence, never proof; a sample this low can still happen when $p = 0.40$.

items.q: What does one dot in the dotplot represent?
options: The proportion made in one simulated set of 50 shots
One of the player's 50 real free throws
The proportion made by the player in one real practice week
The probability that the player is a 75% shooter

why.correct: Each dot is the sample proportion from one simulated set of 50 shots, made in a world where $H_0$ is true ($p = 0.75$).
options: Right: one simulated sample, assuming $H_0$ is true.
The real shots give one value, 0.62. The dots come from the simulation.
The player has one real week of data; the 100 dots are simulated.
The dots are simulated sample proportions, not probabilities about the player.

items.q: Use the dotplot to estimate the p-value of the test.
options: About 0.03: 3 of 100 dots are at or below 0.62
About 0.97, because 97 of the 100 dots are above 0.62
About 0.62, the proportion of shots she made
About 0.75, the center of the dotplot

why.correct: The p-value is the proportion of simulated results at least as extreme as the observed one in the direction of $H_a$ (here, 0.62 or less). 3 of the 100 dots are at or below 0.62, so the estimated p-value is 3/100 = 0.03.
options: Right: count the dots at or beyond the observed value, in the direction of $H_a$.
Those dots are in the wrong direction. $H_a$ says "less than", so count dots at or below 0.62.
That is the observed statistic, not the p-value.
The center is the null value; the p-value is a tail proportion.

items.q: Why is the dotplot centered near 0.75 rather than near 0.62?
options: Because the player's true rate has been shown to be 0.75
Because the simulation assumes $H_0$ is true, $p = 0.75$
Because 100 sets of shots is a large number of samples
Because 0.62 is an outlier in the player's real shooting this week

why.correct: The simulation was run assuming $H_0$ is true, a 75% shooter. A p-value always measures the observed result against what would happen if $H_0$ were true.
options: The simulation assumes 0.75; it does not show it.
Right: the null distribution is built in the world where $H_0$ holds.
The number of simulated sets affects how smooth the dotplot is, not where it is centered.
The real 0.62 is compared with the simulated dots; it does not set their center.

items.q: What does the estimated p-value suggest about the coach's claim?
options: It suggests the coach is right, because most dots are near 0.75
It suggests a lower true rate: 0.62 or less is rare for a 75% shooter
It proves her true free-throw proportion is 0.62
It says nothing, because a simulation is not real data about the player

why.correct: If she really made 75% of her shots, making 62% or fewer in 50 shots happened in about 3 of 100 simulated weeks. That is unusual, so it gives evidence that her true free-throw proportion is less than 0.75.
options: The dots are near 0.75 because they assume the claim; what matters is how rare 0.62 is among them.
Right: a result this rare under $H_0$ is evidence for $H_a$.
A p-value cannot prove anything, and it gives no reason to think the rate is exactly 0.62.
Simulating many samples under $H_0$ and counting extreme results is a valid way to estimate a p-value.

items.q: A website says 20% of visitors click its banner. An analyst takes a random sample of 500 visits, and 116 include a click ($\hat{p} = 0.232$). For $H_0: p = 0.20$ against $H_a: p \ne 0.20$, find the test statistic. Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses $\hat{p} = 0.232$ inside the square root. The test's standard deviation uses $p_0 = 0.20$.

items.q: For the banner test ($z = 1.79$, $H_a: p \ne 0.20$), find the p-value. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is one tail. The alternative is two-sided ($p \ne 0.20$), so double it.
That is the area below $z = 1.79$. Use the tail areas beyond $\pm 1.79$.

why.correct: Two-sided: count both tails. $P(Z \ge 1.79) = 0.0368$, so the p-value is $2(0.0368) = 0.0736$.

items.q: Build the interpretation of the banner test's p-value, 0.0736.

options: Assuming the true proportion of all visits that include a click is 0.20,
Assuming the true proportion of all visits that include a click is 0.232,
Assuming the website's figure is wrong,

why.1: The p-value assumes the null value, 0.20.
why.2: The p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true.

options: there is a 0.0736 probability of getting a sample proportion at least as far from 0.20 as 0.232, in either direction,
there is a 0.0736 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.232 or more,
there is a 0.0736 probability that the website's figure is correct

why.1: That describes one tail, 0.0368. A two-sided p-value counts both directions.
why.2: A p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true.

options: by chance in a random sample of 500 visits.
for the next 500 visitors.
among the 116 clicks.

why.1: The probability is about random samples like the one taken, not a prediction about specific visitors.
why.2: The clicks are the result; the probability is about samples of 500 visits.

conclude.model: Assuming the true proportion of all visits that include a click is 0.20, there is a 0.0736 probability of getting a sample proportion at least as far from 0.20 as 0.232, in either direction, by chance in a random sample of 500 visits.

why.correct: For a two-sided test, "as extreme" means at least as far from $p_0$ in either direction.

items.q: A test of $H_0: p = 0.5$ gives a p-value of 0.31. Which statement is correct?
options: The data show that $p = 0.5$
There is a 31% chance that $p = 0.5$
Results like this are common if $p = 0.5$: little evidence against $H_0$
31% of the people in the sample agreed with the null hypothesis

why.correct: A p-value of 0.31 means results like this one happen about 31% of the time when $H_0$ is true. That is not unusual, so the data give little evidence against $H_0$. It does not show that $H_0$ is true.
options: A large p-value means the data are consistent with $H_0$; it does not prove $H_0$.
The p-value assumes $p = 0.5$; it is not the probability that $p = 0.5$.
Right: a large p-value means the result is not surprising under $H_0$.
A p-value is a probability about samples, not a share of the sample.

items.q: Two studies test $H_0: p = 0.6$ against $H_a: p > 0.6$ with the same sample size. Study 1 finds $\hat{p} = 0.64$ and Study 2 finds $\hat{p} = 0.70$. Which has the smaller p-value, and why?
options: Study 1, because 0.64 is closer to 0.6
They are equal, because the two studies use the same hypotheses
Study 2: 0.70 is farther above 0.6, in the direction of $H_a$
It depends on $\alpha$

why.correct: With the same $n$, the standard deviation $\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/n}$ is the same, so the result farther above 0.6 in the direction of $H_a$ gives a larger $z$ and a smaller tail area.
options: Closer to the null value means less surprising, so a larger p-value.
The hypotheses match, but the observed results differ, so the p-values differ.
Right: a more extreme result under $H_0$ gives a smaller p-value.
The p-value comes from the data and $H_0$; $\alpha$ is only compared with it later.

items.q: The reference sheet gives a standardized test statistic as $\frac{\text{statistic} - \text{parameter}}{\text{standard error of the statistic}}$. In a one-sample z test for a proportion, which values fill it in?
options: $\frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}}$

why.correct: The statistic is $\hat{p}$, the parameter is its value under $H_0$, $p_0$, and the denominator is the standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ computed with $p_0$.
options: Right: everything about the parameter uses $p_0$.
That is the interval's standard error. A test assumes $H_0$, so it uses $p_0$.
The order is statistic minus null value, or the sign comes out backward.
The denominator is a standard deviation, so it needs the square root.

items.q: A test of $H_0: p = 0.3$ against $H_a: p > 0.3$ gives $\hat{p} = 0.34$. Which changes would make the p-value smaller? Select all that apply.
options: The same $\hat{p}$ from a larger random sample
A sample proportion of 0.38 with the same sample size
Using $H_a: p \ne 0.3$ instead
A sample proportion of 0.26 with the same sample size

why.correct: A p-value gets smaller when the result is more extreme in the direction of $H_a$: a larger sample (smaller standard deviation, larger $z$) or a sample proportion farther above 0.3.
options: Right: a larger $n$ shrinks the standard deviation, so $z$ grows.
Right: farther above 0.3 in the direction of $H_a$.
A two-sided p-value counts both tails, so it doubles.
0.26 is below 0.3, the opposite of the direction of $H_a$, so the p-value is large.

items.q: A student writes: "The p-value is 0.02, so there is a 2% chance that the null hypothesis is true." What is the error?
options: There is no error
It should say 98%, the complement, is the chance that $H_a$ is true
The p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true, so it is not the chance $H_0$ is true
A p-value has to be compared with 0.5 before it means anything

why.correct: The p-value is computed by assuming $H_0$ is true. It is the probability of data this extreme or more under $H_0$, not the probability that $H_0$ holds.
options: This is the most common misreading of a p-value.
The complement is not the probability that $H_a$ is true either.
Right: the condition is "if $H_0$ is true", not "that $H_0$ is true".
A p-value is compared with $\alpha$, chosen in advance, not with 0.5.
